extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, political reformers, students and scholars of state government and public administration
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance and standards for reorganizing state (and local) government to increase administrative efficiency and concentrate responsibility. Covers design choices (executive vs. legislative dominance), referendum limits, civil service architecture, selection and powers of departmental chiefs, and recall/accountability mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of power and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle is that both power and responsibility in affairs of local government should be peculiarly concentrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentration requires simplification of machinery and giving either the legislature or the executive a dominant authority. It should be pursued by successive experimental attempts rather than a single rigid plan. The aim is clearer accountability (mistakes or abuses have unmistakable responsibility) and sufficient machinery for victorious reformers to implement policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate choice of subordination (executive vs. legislature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentration of responsibility can be brought about either by subordinating the legislature to the executive or the executive to the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both methods have precedents and comparative advantages. Subordination of the executive to the legislature (parliamentary model) has theoretical merits but faces practical obstacles in the U.S. context (poor quality of small-district representation, entrenched American political traditions). The text favors executive dominance given current realities, but stresses experimentation and careful consideration of representative quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish popular vs. delegated legislative functions (referendum limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The part to be retained by the people is the function of accepting or rejecting certain general proposals respecting state organization or policy; technical details and amendments requiring special knowledge should be delegated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voters are competent to decide broad policy questions (e.g., gambling, liquor laws, commission powers) but not to resolve technical amendments or detailed drafting. Efficient law-making requires experts for detail; therefore referendum/direct legislation should be limited to general policy questions while detailed preparation should be left to representative/technical bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organized control over citizen-initiated legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some organized control over the legislative proposals submitted to popular approval is absolutely necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unrestricted initiative (any group proposing laws) risks bombarding the electorate with poorly drawn, ill-considered, or fringe measures. The proposed control: allow an executive (governor) and a legislative/administrative council to mediate which proposals reach popular vote, with the governor empowered to introduce legislation into the council and bills introduced by the governor given precedence; council retains right of rejection or amendment, and rejected/controversial items may be submitted to popular vote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of a legislative/administrative council of experts
rubrics_metrics.description: The function of the representative body, under a system of direct legislation, is substantially that of a legislative and administrative council or commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a council should be an experienced body of legal, administrative, and financial experts, comparatively limited in numbers, and selected in a manner to make them solicitous of the interests of the whole state. They should be elected from comparatively large districts or statewide (possibly by cumulative voting). Their duty is to prepare legislation for popular enactment or rejection and to act as a technical advisory commission mediating between governor and people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governor-initiated legislation as a control mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: The governor should be empowered not merely to suggest legislation to the council, but to introduce it into the council.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governor-introduced bills need not be exclusive but should receive precedence and a definite amount of the council's time. The council may reject or amend; if rejected or amended unacceptably, the matter would be submitted to popular vote. This method formalizes existing unofficial practice where reform legislation often originates in executive mansions and increases accountability (governors must announce policies during campaigns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve quality of legislative representation (district size & selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: The existing practice of small districts tends to give mediocrity to American popular representation; representatives are seldom capable of drafting bills or dealing intelligently with technical or financial detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To obtain a more effective body for the auxiliary legislative work, members should be elected from larger districts or statewide, perhaps using cumulative voting, thereby encouraging more expert, statewide-minded representatives rather than petty local agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit legislatures to appropriate functions and supply auxiliary machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a large part of government work which must be delegated because it can be efficiently exercised only by peculiarly experienced or competent men; representative bodies must prepare legislation for referendum and handle administrative legislative work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existing legislatures have ceased to be deliberative; therefore any system with direct legislation must create auxiliary machinery (the council) to handle details, supply technical expertise, and prepare acceptable measures for popular enactment. Without such machinery, direct legislation will not be constructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil service reform must extend to higher grades
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'merit system' as currently implemented protects subordinates but fails because it is not applied to higher grades of the service; chiefs remain partisan and temporary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reform laws have reduced abuses at lower levels but not produced efficiency because department heads are appointed/elected for partisan reasons, serve short terms, and can undermine permanent staff. Effective reform requires addressing selection and tenure at higher administrative levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departmental chiefs must have absolute responsibility coupled with effective authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The only way in which administrative efficiency can be secured is by means of an organization which makes a departmental chief absolutely responsible for energetic work and economical administration in his office; and no such responsibility can exist as long as his subordinates are independent of him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chiefs need effective control over subordinates—power to promote and degrade (and, if necessary, to remove with Board consent)—so they can be held accountable. Current civil service protections that make subordinates independent of chiefs undermine efficiency by preventing accountability and promoting routine-formalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select departmental chiefs as expert, non-political servants with secure tenure
rubrics_metrics.description: Departmental chiefs must be divorced from political associations, emancipated from political vicissitudes, and their success must depend exclusively upon the excellence of their departmental work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They should not be elected; they should be appointed, installed for an indefinite period, and subject to removal by the chief executive (not by popular election). This encourages expert administrators whose careers depend on administrative performance rather than partisan service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid electing subordinate executive positions
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of electing the incumbents of subordinate executive positions inevitably invites the evasion of responsibility and the selection of the candidate chiefly for partisan service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elected subordinate officials typically serve short terms, lack qualifications, and cannot be held accountable for administrative efficiency. To make departmental chiefs responsible, they should be appointed by and removable by a chief executive who is accountable to the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use recall as an accountability check on powerful officials
rubrics_metrics.description: The action of the governor or of any member of the legislative council could be challenged by the application of the recall. The recall is for this purpose a useful and legitimate political device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recall allows the electorate to displace officials who misuse powers. While recall may reduce independence for short-term or powerless officials, it is appropriate for really responsible and vigorous officials serving comparatively long terms, providing a direct remedy if they cannot justify dubious practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of an integrated executive-centered local government system
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested core: a chief executive elected for a comparatively long term and subject to recall; an executive council (Cabinet) appointed by him; power to introduce legislation into a legislative council; a legislative council elected from large districts (possibly by cumulative voting) with limited functions; popular approval required for substantial legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details: chief executive appoints an executive council (Controller, Attorney General, etc.); councilors are responsible for departments and exercise authority through permanent departmental chiefs; chief executive has power to remove administrative officials and appoint successors; the legislative council mediates, checks the governor, and authorizes appropriations and minor legislation, while major policy requires direct popular approval. Success depends on good faith implementation and public-minded officials; no plan can absolutely guarantee against misuse but transparency and the ability to punish are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge trade-offs and need for experimental adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: No plan of political organization can in the nature of things offer an absolute guarantee that a government will not misuse its powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of unavoidable trade-offs (risk of usurpation vs. need for concentrated responsibility), reforms should be implemented experimentally and incrementally. Systems should build in remedies (recall, popular sanction) and seek to attract capable, public-spirited officials by offering real opportunity for effective achievement.
